Reinforcement Learning is a topic I am really interested in. For the sake of learning, I have been doing some experiments involving RL. In one of them I investigated how a language model's answers to requests for random
numbers change during RL. I am still working on
this project. There are a few problems with the experiments that I need to solve, and **I don't think the results are ready for a research paper yet.**

## The question

In a recent paper, [Samanta et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29933) found that after supervised
fine-tuning (SFT), different prompts give more similar distributions of answers.
The authors describe this as crystallisation, using the phrase "snap-to-grid." My question for this project was: "whether something similar
happens when a model goes through RL without an SFT step first."

## What I did

AllenAI's OLMo 3 release ([Team Olmo, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961)) made it possible for me
to test this. Its RL-Zero Math model was trained on math problems using RL
directly from the base model. I compared the base model with versions saved
at seven points during that training run.

I used 15 tasks, such as "give me a random digit." For each task, I checked
50 different beginnings for the model's answer and aimed for 500
usable replies for each one. I also checked SFT models, including OLMo 2.
In a smaller experiment, I changed the wording of the question instead and
let the model reason before answering.

## What I found

In the main experiment, the distribution for answers became more different across
prompts as training continued. In the final checkpoint, the average difference
was around 3.7 times the base-model's. In this setup, the answer distributions
moved further apart rather than snapping together. In the digit task, different
answer starts led to different favourite digits. But I was measuring
the usable numbers that followed the answer beginnings I used. I still
don't know if the same pattern holds when the model finishes reasoning
and gives its final answer.

The Olmo 3 SFT reference lines in @fig-training are around 1.2, so they do not
show a drop on my measure either. The paper measures something different: the
largest distance from a selected reference distribution. In a separate OLMo 2
check, that measure did drop after SFT, but the result was sensitive to a few
unusual prompts. I need a larger replication before drawing conclusions from
this.

In the smaller experiment, differences between question wordings exceeded
sampling noise on one of seven tasks for the base model, and on all seven from
step 500 onward. This points in the same direction, although most late answers
were forced after the token limit.

## Limitations

There are a few reasons to be careful with this result. Here are some of the limitations:

- I followed one RL Math training run. I still have not checked if an
  independent run or another model family would behave the same way.
- At the final checkpoint only 21% of answers in the main experiment
  gave a usable number. The model often kept generating tokens after that number, so
  it was not necessarily the answer it would give in the end.
- Letting the model reason first did not completely solve this problem. Around
  93% of the final checkpoint's usable answers in the second experiment
  are given after I stopped the model at 2,048 tokens and asked for an answer.
- All the tasks involve picking numbers. I can't make conclusions about
  creativity or diversity more broadly from these tests, and I don't yet
  know why the measured difference grows.

Earlier work by [Karouzos et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16027) has already looked at output
diversity in RL-Zero models. In this project I am testing how the differences
between prompts change during the training.

## What's next

I am continuing the project. The next experiments I am working towards are:

- giving the model more time to finish its replies;
- checking how changing the way I ask for an answer affects the result;
- repeating the test on an independent RL training run.

For now, I have a pattern in these experiments that needs more checking.
I need to test how much of it comes from the way I
ask the model to answer.

References:

- Samanta, K., Holtzman, A., & West, P. (2026). [Towards Physical Intuitions for Alignment Dynamics: A Case Study With Randomness Crystallization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29933).
- Team Olmo (2025). [Olmo 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961).
- Karouzos, C., Tan, X., & Aletras, N. (2026). [Where does output diversity collapse in post-training?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16027).
